# Case Study: ADNI MCI Prediction {#sec-adni}

A neurologist tells a 74-year-old woman and her daughter that the
memory testing shows mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and the
daughter asks what every family asks: will it become Alzheimer's
disease, and how soon? An honest answer is a probability, and the
probability comes from a model fitted to a cohort like the
Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). If that model
counted the participants who left the study early as people who
never progressed, the number the family hears is too low, and
nothing in the code or its output says so. This chapter builds the
compendium for such a model end to end, so that each quiet decision
is written down, pre-specified, and checkable by a reviewer who
cannot see the data.

## The question and the data {#sec-adni-question}

### The research question

The case study predicts conversion from MCI to Alzheimer's disease
(AD) dementia within three years, from baseline sociodemographic,
clinical, and neuropsychological measures. The aim is not to solve
the prediction problem, which would be a book-length exercise, but
to demonstrate the workflow around it: scaffolding, planning,
wrangling, describing, modeling, reporting, and depositing. The
modeling itself is deliberately light; the companion book,
*Statistical Computing in the Age of AI*, covers it.

From the statistical analysis plan (SAP), drafted with the template
of @sec-analysis-plan-template:

> Can baseline sociodemographic characteristics, clinical scales,
> and neuropsychological test scores predict conversion from MCI to
> AD dementia within 3 years?

Two secondary questions come from the same template: which
predictor categories (sociodemographic, clinical,
neuropsychological) contribute most to prediction accuracy, and
whether performance differs between early MCI (EMCI) and late MCI
(LMCI).

MCI is a heterogeneous state. Some people progress to AD within
months; others remain stable for years. Identifying those at
highest risk enables targeted intervention trials, earlier
counseling, and informed family planning. A model with modest
discrimination (an area under the receiver operating
characteristic (ROC) curve, AUC, of 0.75 to 0.80)
is useful clinically; one with an AUC of 0.95 has probably been
trained or evaluated wrong. Prior work [@grassi2019novel] has
established age, education, APOE4 status, and baseline ADAS13 as
reliable predictors; the question is whether a multivariable model
outperforms any one of them.

### The ADNI dataset

ADNI is a longitudinal multicenter cohort study funded since 2004.
Its data are obtained under a data-use agreement (DUA) at
<https://adni.loni.usc.edu/>. The `ADNIMERGE` package is the
community-standard R interface: a single long-format table of
roughly 15,000 visits on about 2,000 participants, with over a
hundred variables spanning demographics, APOE genotype, clinical
scales such as the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) and Functional
Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), and neuropsychological tests.

| Variable | Description | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| `RID` | Participant ID | Integer |
| `VISCODE` | Visit code | `bl`, `m06`, `m12`, ... |
| `DX` | Diagnosis at the visit | CN (cognitively normal), MCI, Dementia |
| `DX_bl` | Baseline diagnosis | CN, SMC (subjective memory complaint), EMCI, LMCI, AD |
| `AGE`, `PTGENDER`, `PTEDUCAT` | Age, sex, years of education | Demographics |
| `APOE4` | Number of APOE $\varepsilon$4 alleles | 0, 1, 2 |
| `ADAS13` | 13-item Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale, cognitive subscale: memory, language, praxis | 0 to 85, higher worse |
| `RAVLT.immediate` | Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, immediate recall: list learning | Higher better |
| `MMSE` | Mini-Mental State Examination: a cognitive screen | 0 to 30, higher better |
| `LDELTOTAL` | Logical Memory II delayed recall: story recall | Higher better |

: Key ADNIMERGE variables for this case study. {#tbl-adni-vars}

APOE $\varepsilon$4 (apolipoprotein E, allele 4) is the most
established genetic risk factor for late-onset AD. Relative to
non-carriers, one copy raises risk roughly three-fold and two
copies roughly eight- to twelve-fold in the large case-control
meta-analyses, with estimates that vary by age, sex, and ancestry.
The instruments are correlated but not redundant: each captures a
different aspect of cognition or risk, and the predictive question
is whether their combination outperforms any one alone.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague reports a cross-validated AUC of 0.96 for
three-year conversion from baseline measures alone. What is your
first hypothesis?

**Answer.** That something leaks. The published range from baseline
clinical and cognitive measures is far lower, and MCI's
heterogeneity limits how well any baseline profile can predict.
Look first for an outcome-derived predictor (a variable measured
after baseline) and for folds that split one participant's visits
across training and test.
:::

## Working under a data-use agreement {#sec-adni-dua}

### Why the compendium matters more here

ADNI analyses have three properties that make reproducibility
harder and more valuable at once, and each has an answer in the
compendium.

| Property | Consequence | What the compendium does |
|---|---|---|
| Data-use agreement | The data cannot be shared | Public code, `renv.lock`, and a synthetic stand-in; collaborators obtain the data under their own DUA |
| Long time horizon | Reviewer requests and follow-up analyses arrive years later | A Docker-pinned environment reruns the original analysis on the same R and package versions |
| Version churn in `ADNIMERGE` | New participants appear and variables are renamed between releases | The installed version recorded in `renv.lock`, the source tarball kept, and a frozen copy of the data file |

: Three properties of ADNI analyses and the compendium's answer to
each. {#tbl-adni-properties}

Data sharing is therefore asymmetric. The code can be public; the
data cannot. The compendium ships in two parts, a public code-only
deposit and the documented route by which a collaborator obtains
the data, and the README states the distinction explicitly.

### Scaffolding

Assemble the compendium by hand (@sec-zzcollab-assemble) or with a
framework. With the in-house `zzcollab` (@sec-zzcollab-optional),
the session is (display-only):

```bash
mkdir adni-mci
cd adni-mci
zzc tidyverse            # scaffold the Five Pillars
make r                   # enter R inside the container
```

`zzcollab` has no modeling profile. Install the modeling packages
inside the container (`glmnet` for penalized regression, `survival`
for time-to-event handling of dropout), record them with
`make snapshot`, and rebuild the image with `make docker-build`.

`ADNIMERGE` is not on CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network)
or public GitHub. It is distributed as a source tarball through the
LONI (Laboratory of Neuro Imaging) Image and Data Archive to
investigators whose data-use application has been approved.[^adnimerge2]
Install the file you downloaded (display-only):

[^adnimerge2]: As of October 2026, ADNI also distributes a
    successor package, `ADNIMERGE2`; check which one your approval
    covers.

```r
renv::install('~/Downloads/ADNIMERGE_0.0.1.tar.gz')
renv::snapshot()
```

`renv.lock` now records the `ADNIMERGE` version, with a local
rather than a repository source. `renv::restore()` cannot download
it for a collaborator: each collaborator obtains the same tarball
from LONI under their own DUA and places it where `renv` looks for
local sources (see `?renv::paths`, `RENV_PATHS_LOCAL`), after which
the restore installs the same version.

Under `analysis/`, the compendium grows:

```
analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/adnimerge_20260301.rds      # frozen copy, gitignored
│   └── derived/
│       ├── analytic_cohort.rds         # one row per RID
│       ├── adnimerge_clean.rds         # visits of the cohort
│       └── predictions.rds             # held-out predictions
├── paper/paper.qmd
└── scripts/
    ├── 00-simulate.R                   # the synthetic stand-in
    ├── 01-build-cohort.R
    ├── 02-table1.R
    ├── 03-trajectories.R
    └── 04-model.R
```

`data/raw/adnimerge_20260301.rds` is a frozen snapshot of the data
on the date of analysis, so the analysis reruns against the same
data even after `ADNIMERGE` updates. The file is gitignored, and
the README documents how a collaborator with DUA access recreates
it.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Participant-level rows leave the enclave without an error.** A
`head(adnimerge)` pasted into a chat window, a CSV attached to an
issue, or a data file committed and pushed to a public repository
each discloses DUA-restricted data, and nothing in R, Git, or the
chat interface stops it. The ADNI DUA limits the data to the uses
in your approved application and forbids passing them on, and a
language-model service is a third party like any other. Send
structure: column names, types, the
schema of the synthetic stand-in, and aggregate summaries. Add the
data directories to `.gitignore` before the first commit, not after
the first push.
:::

### A synthetic stand-in

The real analysis cannot execute in this book, and a reviewer
without a DUA cannot run it either. Both problems have the same
answer: a generator that produces data with the schema of
`ADNIMERGE`, so that every script runs end to end without any ADNI
file present. The generator below writes long-format visits for
the five baseline diagnoses, with conversion to dementia among the
MCI participants depending on APOE4 dose, LMCI status, and baseline
ADAS13, and with dropout that by default does not depend on
anything. Only `ADAS13` changes over time; the other measures are
baseline values repeated, which is all the scripts need.

```{r}
#| label: adni-simulate
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

#' Simulate visit-level data with the ADNIMERGE schema
#'
#' @param n Number of participants.
#' @param seed Random seed.
#' @param dropout_rate Yearly dropout hazard; 0 means no dropout.
#' @param dropout_adas Log-hazard increase in dropout per ADAS13
#'   point above 15; 0 makes dropout uninformative.
#' @return A tibble with one row per visit.
simulate_adnimerge <- function(n = 1500, seed = 41, dropout_rate = 0.12,
                               dropout_adas = 0) {
  set.seed(seed)
  dx_bl <- sample(c('CN', 'SMC', 'EMCI', 'LMCI', 'AD'), n,
                  replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.10, 0.25, 0.30, 0.10))
  apoe4 <- sample(0:2, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.36, 0.09))
  adas_bl <- pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, c(CN = 9, SMC = 9, EMCI = 12,
                                      LMCI = 18, AD = 30)[dx_bl], 5)))
  # conversion risk rises with APOE4 dose, LMCI, and ADAS13: the
  # associations the analysis is meant to find
  rate <- exp(-2.6 + 0.5 * apoe4 + 0.6 * (dx_bl == 'LMCI') +
                0.05 * (adas_bl - 15))
  t_convert <- ifelse(dx_bl %in% c('EMCI', 'LMCI'), rexp(n, rate), Inf)
  # scaling one draw keeps the same participants when the rate is 0
  t_drop <- rexp(n) / (dropout_rate * exp(dropout_adas * (adas_bl - 15)))

  tibble(
    RID = seq_len(n), DX_bl = dx_bl, APOE4 = apoe4,
    AGE = round(rnorm(n, 73, 7), 1),
    PTGENDER = sample(c('Male', 'Female'), n, replace = TRUE),
    PTEDUCAT = pmin(20L, pmax(6L, as.integer(round(rnorm(n, 16, 2.7))))),
    RAVLT.immediate = as.integer(pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, 45 - adas_bl, 8)))),
    MMSE = as.integer(pmin(30, pmax(18, round(30 - adas_bl / 6 +
                                               rnorm(n, 0, 1.5))))),
    LDELTOTAL = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.04, NA_integer_,
                       as.integer(pmax(0, round(rnorm(n, 14 - adas_bl / 2,
                                                      3))))),
    bl_date = as.Date('2010-01-01') + sample(0:2500, n, replace = TRUE),
    adas_bl = adas_bl, t_convert = t_convert, t_drop = t_drop
  ) |>
    tidyr::crossing(month = c(0, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48)) |>
    filter(month == 0 | month / 12 <= t_drop) |>
    mutate(
      years = month / 12,
      VISCODE = ifelse(month == 0, 'bl', sprintf('m%02d', month)),
      # ADNI visit windows: a scheduled visit can fall weeks early or late
      EXAMDATE = bl_date + round(month * 30.44) +
        ifelse(month == 0, 0, sample(-45:45, n(), replace = TRUE)),
      DX = case_when(
        DX_bl == 'AD' ~ 'Dementia',
        DX_bl %in% c('CN', 'SMC') ~ 'CN',
        years >= t_convert ~ 'Dementia',
        .default = 'MCI'
      ),
      DX = ifelse(month > 0 & runif(n()) < 0.05, NA, DX),
      ADAS13 = round(pmax(0, adas_bl + years * (1 + 0.8 * APOE4 +
                                                  3 * (years >= t_convert)) +
                            rnorm(n(), 0, 2.5)), 1)
    ) |>
    select(RID, VISCODE, EXAMDATE, DX_bl, DX, AGE, PTGENDER, PTEDUCAT,
           APOE4, ADAS13, RAVLT.immediate, MMSE, LDELTOTAL)
}

adnimerge <- simulate_adnimerge()
glimpse(adnimerge)
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The assertions, not the generator, are the deliverable. A reviewer
needs to know the synthetic frame can stand in for the real one,
and that claim is made by checking it:

```{r}
#| label: adni-simulate-verify
stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(adnimerge[c('RID', 'VISCODE')]),
  all(adnimerge$DX_bl %in% c('CN', 'SMC', 'EMCI', 'LMCI', 'AD')),
  all(adnimerge$DX %in% c('CN', 'MCI', 'Dementia', NA)),
  all(adnimerge$APOE4 %in% 0:2),
  all(adnimerge$MMSE >= 0 & adnimerge$MMSE <= 30),
  all(adnimerge$ADAS13 >= 0 & adnimerge$ADAS13 <= 85),
  inherits(adnimerge$EXAMDATE, 'Date'),
  all(table(adnimerge$RID[adnimerge$VISCODE == 'bl']) == 1)
)
```

Three rules apply to every generator of this kind. Schema
constraints (types, levels, ranges, one baseline per participant)
matter more than distributions; whether `ADAS13` is realistic is
irrelevant, and pretending otherwise invites the generator to be
mistaken for a model of the disease. Build in the associations the
analysis claims to find, because a pure-noise generator runs the
pipeline without exercising it. And never present synthetic output
as a result: every number computed from `adnimerge` in this
chapter recovers parameters written into the generator, which
checks the code and says nothing about Alzheimer's disease.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks for 'the data' so that they can
check your code. What can you send, and what can you not?

**Answer.** You can send the public compendium (code, `renv.lock`,
Dockerfile, README) and the synthetic generator with its
assertions, which together let the reviewer run every script. You
cannot send ADNI data, extracts, or derived participant-level
files, however small, because the DUA does not permit it. A
reviewer who needs the real data applies to ADNI and runs the same
code.
:::

## Building the analytic cohort {#sec-adni-cohort}

### From visits to one row per participant

In the real project, `scripts/01-build-cohort.R` begins
(display-only):

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(ADNIMERGE)
raw <- adnimerge
```

Everything after that line runs unchanged against the synthetic
`adnimerge`. The cohort logic is wrapped in a function so that it
can be tested (exercise 6).

```{r}
#| label: adni-build-cohort
predictors <- c('AGE', 'PTGENDER', 'PTEDUCAT', 'APOE4', 'ADAS13',
                'RAVLT.immediate', 'MMSE', 'LDELTOTAL')

#' Derive the three-year conversion outcome for baseline MCI
#'
#' @param raw Visit-level data with the ADNIMERGE schema.
#' @param horizon_days Length of the outcome window.
#' @param tolerance_days How early a month-36 visit may fall and
#'   still close the window.
#' @return One row per baseline EMCI or LMCI participant, with
#'   `converted_by_3y`, `last_dx_days`, and `outcome_observed`.
build_cohort <- function(raw, horizon_days = 3 * 365.25,
                         tolerance_days = 90) {
  baseline <- raw |>
    filter(VISCODE == 'bl', DX_bl %in% c('EMCI', 'LMCI')) |>
    select(RID, all_of(predictors), DX_bl, EXAMDATE)

  visits <- raw |>
    filter(RID %in% baseline$RID) |>
    arrange(RID, EXAMDATE) |>
    group_by(RID) |>
    mutate(days_since_bl = as.numeric(EXAMDATE - first(EXAMDATE))) |>
    ungroup()

  followup <- visits |>
    group_by(RID) |>
    summarize(
      converted_by_3y = any(DX == 'Dementia' &
                              days_since_bl <= horizon_days,
                            na.rm = TRUE),
      last_dx_days    = max(days_since_bl[!is.na(DX)]),
      .groups = 'drop'
    )

  # outcome observed: converted within 3 years (whenever they left),
  # or followed through the 3-year visit without converting
  baseline |>
    left_join(followup, by = 'RID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |>
    mutate(outcome_observed = converted_by_3y |
             last_dx_days >= horizon_days - tolerance_days)
}

cohort <- build_cohort(adnimerge)

analytic_cohort <- cohort |>
  filter(outcome_observed) |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(predictors), \(x) !is.na(x))) |>
  mutate(converted_3y = converted_by_3y) |>
  select(RID, all_of(predictors), DX_bl, EXAMDATE, converted_3y)

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(analytic_cohort$RID),
          !anyNA(analytic_cohort$converted_3y))

# long-format visits of the same participants, for trajectories
adnimerge_clean <- adnimerge |>
  filter(RID %in% analytic_cohort$RID) |>
  group_by(RID) |>
  mutate(
    years_since_baseline = as.numeric(EXAMDATE - min(EXAMDATE)) / 365.25,
    visit_month = as.integer(sub('^m', '', sub('^bl$', 'm0', VISCODE))),
    APOE4_any = factor(APOE4 > 0, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                       labels = c('No APOE4 allele', 'Any APOE4 allele'))
  ) |>
  ungroup()

derived <- file.path(tempdir(), 'derived')
dir.create(derived, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(analytic_cohort, file.path(derived, 'analytic_cohort.rds'))
saveRDS(adnimerge_clean, file.path(derived, 'adnimerge_clean.rds'))
```

In the project, `derived` is `analysis/data/derived`. The
non-obvious step is `outcome_observed`. A participant who converted
within three years is a converter whether or not they stayed in
the study afterward. A participant who has not converted counts as
a non-converter only if followed through the three-year visit; one
who left earlier without converting has an unobserved outcome.

The code excludes those participants, which is simple and common,
and which removes the misclassification. It is not neutral.
Converters who left early stay in, while non-converters who left
early go, so the excluded cohort over-represents converters and
overstates the three-year risk, by less than counting dropouts as
non-converters understates it (exercise 1 measures both). The
alternative is a time-to-event analysis that censors early leavers
at their last visit: a Kaplan-Meier estimate for the three-year
risk, and a Cox or discrete-time model for prediction, which are
unbiased when dropout is unrelated to the risk of conversion. The
SAP pre-specifies which is primary, the other is a sensitivity
analysis, and the excluded count goes in the follow-up box of
@fig-adni-cohort.

```{r}
#| label: adni-naive-rate
#| echo: false
naive_pct <- round(100 * mean(cohort$converted_by_3y))
correct_pct <- round(100 * mean(analytic_cohort$converted_3y))
n_unobserved <- sum(!cohort$outcome_observed)
```

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Dropouts counted as non-converters lower the risk without an
error.** Skip the `outcome_observed` filter and every one of the
`r n_unobserved` participants who left early without converting
becomes a non-converter. On the synthetic data the three-year
conversion proportion is then `r naive_pct`%, against
`r correct_pct`% among participants whose outcome was observed
(exercise 1 compares both with the truth), and every model fitted
to that outcome inherits the understatement. The code runs, the
table looks plausible, and the family in the opening hears a
number that is too low.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft the inclusion and exclusion section of the
SAP, and check it against the code.

> **Context.** Below are the 'Cohort definition' template from my
> SAP and the variable table of the ADNIMERGE schema (names,
> types, levels; no data). The population is participants with
> baseline EMCI or LMCI; the outcome is a diagnosis of dementia at
> any visit within three years of baseline. Visits fall up to 90
> days from schedule.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not treat participants who leave before
> three years without converting as non-converters. Keep a
> participant who converted and then left as a converter.
>
> **Criteria.** Write each criterion so that it maps to one
> filter in code. List, for each criterion, the count the
> manuscript must report. State the alternative to exclusion
> (censoring in a time-to-event analysis) and the question it
> answers instead.

*Failure mode.* Models often write 'participants with at least
three years of follow-up', which wrongly excludes early converters
who then left, or 'participants who did not convert were
classified as stable', which reintroduces the dropout bias.
*Check.* Translate each drafted criterion into a filter, run it on
the synthetic data, and compare its counts with @tbl-adni-flow;
then have a clinical collaborator read the draft. Send the
template and the schema, never rows (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### The cohort flow

The analytic cohort is not the enrolled cohort, and the gap between
the two is itself a reportable result. @fig-adni-cohort traces the
derivation in the manner of a CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of
Reporting Trials) flow diagram, and @tbl-adni-flow gives the counts
the code produced. Each exclusion is a number the manuscript must
state, because a reader cannot judge selection bias without it.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-adni-cohort
%%| fig-alt: "CONSORT-style vertical flow of cohort derivation. The
%%|   full ADNIMERGE roster narrows to participants with baseline
%%|   EMCI or LMCI, excluding CN, SMC and AD; then to those with
%%|   three-year follow-up or conversion, excluding insufficient
%%|   follow-up; then to those with key predictors observed,
%%|   excluding or imputing per the SAP; and finally to the analytic
%%|   cohort."
%%| fig-cap: "Cohort-derivation flow for the ADNI analysis, in the
%%|   CONSORT style. Every arrow is an exclusion with a count the
%%|   manuscript must report; the analytic cohort is smaller than the
%%|   enrolled cohort, and by how much is itself a finding."
flowchart TD
  A["ADNIMERGE roster<br/><i>all participants</i>"] --> B["Baseline EMCI or LMCI<br/><i>exclude CN, SMC, AD</i>"]
  B --> C["3-year follow-up or conversion<br/><i>exclude insufficient follow-up</i>"]
  C --> D["Key predictors observed<br/><i>exclude, or impute per SAP</i>"]
  D --> E["Analytic cohort"]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-adni-flow
#| tbl-cap: "Counts at each step of the cohort derivation, synthetic
#|   data. The real counts come from the same code run on
#|   ADNIMERGE."
flow <- tibble(
  step = c('Roster', 'Baseline EMCI or LMCI',
           'Outcome observed within 3 years', 'Predictors complete'),
  n = c(n_distinct(adnimerge$RID), nrow(cohort),
        sum(cohort$outcome_observed), nrow(analytic_cohort))
) |>
  mutate(excluded = ifelse(is.na(lag(n)), '', format(lag(n) - n)))
knitr::kable(flow)
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that every participant excluded for follow-up neither
converted within the window nor reached the three-year visit, and
that every participant kept satisfies one or the other.

```{r}
#| label: adni-cohort-verify
excluded <- filter(cohort, !outcome_observed)
stopifnot(
  !any(excluded$converted_by_3y),
  all(excluded$last_dx_days < 3 * 365.25 - 90),
  all(analytic_cohort$RID %in% cohort$RID[cohort$outcome_observed]),
  nrow(analytic_cohort) == tail(flow$n, 1)
)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A participant attends only the baseline and 12-month
visits, then drops out, diagnosed MCI at both. How should they
appear in the analysis of the three-year outcome?

**Answer.** They were observed event-free for one year, not three,
so their three-year outcome is unknown. Treating them as a
non-converter is wrong, and biases the risk downward. Two options
remain. *Censor* them at month 12 in a time-to-event analysis,
which keeps the year they were observed; the Kaplan-Meier estimate
at three years is then the three-year risk. Or *exclude* them, as
the code does; the cohort becomes participants who either converted
within three years or were followed through the three-year visit
(a shorter threshold, such as 24 months, would readmit the
problem), at the cost of the upward bias described above. The SAP
names one option as primary and the other as a sensitivity
analysis.
:::

### Exercises

1. Compare four estimates of the three-year conversion risk on
   synthetic data where the truth is known: the proportion with no
   dropout at all (`dropout_rate = 0`, the target); dropouts
   counted as non-converters; dropouts excluded; and the
   Kaplan-Meier estimate with dropouts censored. Average over 20
   simulated cohorts so that the pattern is not one draw's noise.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-24-1
km_risk <- function(raw, horizon_days = 3 * 365.25) {
  event_times <- raw |>
    filter(DX_bl %in% c('EMCI', 'LMCI')) |>
    arrange(RID, EXAMDATE) |>
    group_by(RID) |>
    mutate(days = as.numeric(EXAMDATE - first(EXAMDATE))) |>
    summarize(
      event = any(DX == 'Dementia', na.rm = TRUE),
      time = if (event) min(days[DX %in% 'Dementia'])
             else max(days[!is.na(DX)]),
      .groups = 'drop'
    )
  km <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, event) ~ 1,
                          data = event_times)
  1 - summary(km, times = horizon_days)$surv
}

risk_estimates <- function(seed) {
  observed <- simulate_adnimerge(seed = seed)
  target <- build_cohort(simulate_adnimerge(seed = seed,
                                            dropout_rate = 0))
  sim_cohort <- build_cohort(observed)
  100 * c(
    target   = mean(target$converted_by_3y),
    naive    = mean(sim_cohort$converted_by_3y),
    excluded = mean(sim_cohort$converted_by_3y[
      sim_cohort$outcome_observed]),
    censored = km_risk(observed)
  )
}

risk <- rowMeans(sapply(1:20, risk_estimates))
round(risk, 1)
```

With no dropout every outcome is observed, so the first number is
the target, `r round(risk[['target']], 1)`%. Counting dropouts as
non-converters gives `r round(risk[['naive']], 1)`%, far below it.
Excluding them gives `r round(risk[['excluded']], 1)`%, above it:
early converters who left are kept and early non-converters who
left are not, so converters are over-represented. The
Kaplan-Meier estimate, `r round(risk[['censored']], 1)`%, is
closest, because censoring uses each participant's observed time
without guessing the outcome after it; its remaining gap is small
next to the other two errors. Censoring relies on dropout being
unrelated to the risk of conversion, as it is in this generator.
When it may not be, rerun the comparison with
`dropout_adas = 0.08` and plan a sensitivity analysis accordingly.
:::

## Describing the cohort {#sec-adni-describe}

### Table 1

`gtsummary` [@sjoberg2021gtsummary] builds the Table 1 from the
analytic cohort. Two choices need stating. `APOE4` is stored as
0, 1, 2 and is summarized as counts, not as a mean, so it is
declared categorical. `ADAS13` is right-skewed in MCI cohorts, so
continuous variables are summarized as median and quartiles, which
is `gtsummary`'s default.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-adni-table1
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of the synthetic analytic
#|   cohort by three-year conversion, median (first quartile, third
#|   quartile) or n (%)."
#| message: false
library(gtsummary)

analytic_cohort |>
  mutate(converted_3y = factor(converted_3y, c(FALSE, TRUE),
                               c('Did not convert', 'Converted'))) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = converted_3y,
    include = c(AGE, PTGENDER, PTEDUCAT, APOE4, ADAS13, MMSE, DX_bl),
    type = list(APOE4 ~ 'categorical')
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  as_kable()
```

A descriptive Table 1 carries no row p-values. The in-house
`zztable1` package (@sec-lab-software) offers a similar formula
interface with journal styles (`console`, `nejm`, `lancet`, `jama`,
`bmj`, `simple`), but as of this writing it leaves the
missing-value row blank instead of reporting the count where a
variable like `APOE4` has missing values. Use `gtsummary` until
that is fixed. Whichever tool you use, match the target journal's
template.

### Cognitive trajectories

The trajectory plot is a sanity check that the cohort behaves as
the literature says it should. `ggplot2` draws it from the
visit-level data; the mean and a 95% confidence interval at each
scheduled visit are computed first, so the plot shows exactly the
numbers in the summary.

```{r}
#| label: fig-adni-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Mean ADAS13 by scheduled visit, by baseline diagnosis,
#|   for participants with and without an APOE4 allele, with 95%
#|   confidence intervals. Synthetic data: the pattern recovers the
#|   generator's parameters."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, no APOE4 allele and any APOE4 allele. Each
#|   shows mean ADAS13 from baseline to month 48 for EMCI and LMCI
#|   participants. LMCI lines start higher than EMCI lines, all
#|   lines rise over time, and they rise more steeply in the
#|   APOE4-carrier panel. Intervals widen at later visits."
#| fig-scap: "ADAS13 trajectories by baseline diagnosis and APOE4"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
library(ggplot2)

trajectory <- adnimerge_clean |>
  group_by(APOE4_any, DX_bl, visit_month) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(ADAS13), se = sd(ADAS13) / sqrt(n()),
            n = n(), .groups = 'drop')

ggplot(trajectory, aes(visit_month, mean, color = DX_bl)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
                  size = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ APOE4_any) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Dark2') +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48)) +
  labs(x = 'Months since baseline', y = 'ADAS13 (higher is worse)',
       color = 'Baseline') +
  theme_minimal()
```

LMCI participants start worse than EMCI participants, and within
each, APOE4 carriers worsen faster. Both observations are expected
from the literature (and here, from the generator); if the real
cohort did not show them, the cohort derivation would be the first
suspect. The later visits average over fewer participants, the
ones who stayed, which is the dropout problem again in graphical
form.

One way to automate a trial-style version of this figure is the
in-house `zzlongplot` package (@sec-lab-software). Its formula
reads outcome by time, split after the bar by group, and
`cluster_var` names the column that identifies a participant
(display-only):

```r
zzlongplot::lplot(
  adnimerge_clean,
  form = ADAS13 ~ visit_month | DX_bl,
  facet_form = ~ APOE4_any,
  cluster_var = 'RID',
  summary_statistic = 'mean',
  confidence_interval = 0.95,
  clinical_mode = TRUE,
  theme = 'fda',
  xlab = 'Months since baseline',
  ylab = 'ADAS13'
)
```

`theme` selects a publication style (`fda`, `nejm`, `lancet`,
`jama`, `nature`, `science`, `jco`).[^fda-theme]

[^fda-theme]: `fda` is the package's label for a plain,
    high-contrast style intended for clinical study reports. The
    FDA (US Food and Drug Administration) publishes no figure style
    standard; its PDF specifications constrain page size, fonts,
    and resolution of submitted documents, not the look of a plot.

### Exercises

2. Add a second table to the compendium comparing baseline
   cognitive scores (`ADAS13`, `RAVLT.immediate`, `MMSE`,
   `LDELTOTAL`) between EMCI and LMCI participants, with means and
   standard deviations, and produce it as both a Markdown and an
   HTML table.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-24-2
#| message: false
table_cog <- analytic_cohort |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = DX_bl,
    include = c(ADAS13, RAVLT.immediate, MMSE, LDELTOTAL),
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ '{mean} ({sd})'
  )
as_kable(table_cog)
html_file <- file.path(tempdir(), 'table-cognition.html')
gt::gtsave(as_gt(table_cog), html_file)
file.exists(html_file)
```

`statistic` overrides the default median and quartiles for every
continuous variable at once. One `tbl_summary()` object renders to
any format (`as_kable()`, `as_gt()`, `as_flex_table()` for Word),
so the table is computed once and only its rendering differs.
State in the caption which summary you used, because means and
medians of a skewed score can differ by several points.
:::

3. Draw the ADAS13 trajectory stratified by three-year conversion
   rather than baseline diagnosis, and save it at 300 DPI (dots
   per inch) for journal submission.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-24-3
#| fig-show: hide
by_outcome <- adnimerge_clean |>
  left_join(select(analytic_cohort, RID, converted_3y), by = 'RID',
            relationship = 'many-to-one') |>
  group_by(converted_3y, visit_month) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(ADAS13), se = sd(ADAS13) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = 'drop')

p <- ggplot(by_outcome, aes(visit_month, mean, color = converted_3y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se)) +
  labs(x = 'Months since baseline', y = 'ADAS13',
       color = 'Converted by 3 years') +
  theme_minimal()

out <- file.path(tempdir(), 'adas13-by-outcome.png')
ggsave(out, p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
dim(png::readPNG(out))
```

The saved file is 1,800 by 1,200 pixels, six by four inches at 300
DPI. Converters' curves rise more steeply, as they must, because
the outcome partly defines the trajectory: a plot stratified by an
outcome measured later describes the outcome, and it is not
evidence that baseline measures predict it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why is `APOE4` declared categorical in the Table 1
call, when it is a count?

**Answer.** Because a mean of 0.6 alleles describes no participant
and hides the share of homozygotes, which is the clinically
important group. As n (%) for 0, 1, and 2 alleles, the table shows
the distribution a reader needs. `gtsummary` would otherwise treat
a numeric column with three values as categorical anyway; stating
it makes the choice visible and stable if a future extract has
only two observed values.
:::

## The pre-specified analysis plan {#sec-adni-sap}

ADNI is large and well studied, so an unprincipled analyst can
find any signal they want in it. The SAP, written before the
analytic cohort is opened (@sec-analysis-plan), locks the predictor
set, the model class, the validation strategy, and the metrics;
anything not pre-specified is exploratory. For ADNI, the SAP
template of @sec-analysis-plan-template has sections for background
and rationale; research questions; cohort definition; exposure,
outcome, and covariate definitions; the primary analysis; secondary
analyses; missing-data handling; and sensitivity analyses.
@tbl-adni-prespecified separates what is locked from what is
exploratory.

| Element | Pre-specified (locked before data access) | Exploratory (documented, not pre-specified) |
|---|---|---|
| Predictors | The eight baseline predictors in the cohort script, `AGE` through `LDELTOTAL`; no additions during model selection | Variable-importance plot from the fitted model |
| Model | Penalized logistic regression with elastic net, tuning $\alpha \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}$ and a grid of $\lambda$ | Other model classes, reported as such |
| Validation | 10-fold cross-validation at the participant level; outer 80/20 holdout for final performance | Repeated or nested resampling |
| Metrics | AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence interval (CI; 1,000 resamples); calibration plot with calibration slope and intercept, as TRIPOD+AI expects | Decision-curve analysis |
| Threshold | Youden index on the training data, held fixed for evaluation; sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV at that threshold | Alternative thresholds |
| Subgroups | None | Performance by EMCI and LMCI |
| Missing data | Complete case for predictors, with counts; dropout handled as in @sec-adni-cohort | Multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis |

: Pre-specified versus exploratory elements of the ADNI SAP. PPV
and NPV are the positive and negative predictive values.
{#tbl-adni-prespecified}

The distinction is what makes the primary finding valid: it was
not selected on the basis of having looked at the data. Tag the SAP
commit before the cohort is built (@sec-analysis-plan-tagging), so
that the order is provable.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Draft the SAP's missing-data section with a model, sending only an
aggregate profile.

> **Context.** Prediction model for three-year MCI-to-AD
> conversion; eight baseline predictors. Missingness profile
> (aggregate counts only): `LDELTOTAL` missing in 4% of the
> cohort, other predictors complete; dropout before three years in
> about 30% of participants. No participant-level data are
> attached.
>
> **Constraints.** Do not recommend an approach by the fraction
> missing alone. Do not describe complete-case analysis as biased
> under MAR as a rule.
>
> **Criteria.** For predictor missingness, state the condition
> under which complete case gives unbiased coefficients and what
> it costs in precision; specify multiple imputation with the
> outcome in the imputation model as the sensitivity analysis.
> Name at least one analysis of sensitivity to data missing not at
> random (MNAR). Handle dropout separately from predictor
> missingness.

*Failure mode.* Models recommend multiple imputation because '30%
is a lot', call complete case biased whenever data are missing at
random (MAR), or merge dropout (an outcome problem) with predictor
missingness. *Check.* Compare the draft with
@sec-missing-complete-case: complete case is unbiased for the
coefficients when missingness does not depend on the outcome given
the covariates, whatever the fraction. Check the DUA before sending
anything, and send aggregates, never rows (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** After fitting the pre-specified model, you find that
adding hippocampal volume raises the AUC by 0.04. Can it go in the
primary analysis?

**Answer.** No. It was not in the locked predictor set, and a
predictor added after seeing performance turns the primary
analysis into a selected one. Report it as exploratory, labeled as
such, with the pre-specified model as the primary result. If it
matters, it is the primary hypothesis of the next study's SAP.
:::

## Modeling on the synthetic cohort {#sec-adni-model}

### Participant-level validation

Cross-validation that splits at the observation level leaks
information whenever a participant contributes several rows: the
same person sits in training and test, and the AUC is optimistic
in a way no held-out evaluation can match. The analytic cohort has
exactly one row per `RID`, so ordinary fold assignment is already
participant-level here. The rule bites as soon as a later visit
enters the modeling frame; then assign folds by `RID`, which in
`tidymodels` is `rsample::group_vfold_cv(group = RID)`.
`rsample::vfold_cv(strata = converted_3y)` stratifies, preserving
the class balance across folds, but it does not group.

The code below runs the pre-specified analysis with `glmnet`
directly, assigning folds explicitly so that their level is visible.
In the project it is `scripts/04-model.R`.

```{r}
#| label: adni-model
#| message: false
library(glmnet)

set.seed(2026)
test_rid <- analytic_cohort |>
  group_by(converted_3y) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.2) |>
  pull(RID)
train <- filter(analytic_cohort, !RID %in% test_rid)
test  <- filter(analytic_cohort, RID %in% test_rid)

design <- function(d) {
  model.matrix(reformulate(predictors), data = d)[, -1]
}
foldid <- sample(rep_len(1:10, nrow(train)))

fits <- lapply(c(0, 0.5, 1), \(a) {
  cv.glmnet(design(train), train$converted_3y, family = 'binomial',
            alpha = a, foldid = foldid)
})
best <- fits[[which.min(vapply(fits, \(f) min(f$cvm), numeric(1)))]]

p_train <- as.numeric(predict(best, design(train), s = 'lambda.min',
                              type = 'response'))
p_test  <- as.numeric(predict(best, design(test), s = 'lambda.min',
                              type = 'response'))

predictions <- tibble(RID = test$RID, observed = test$converted_3y,
                      predicted = p_test)
saveRDS(predictions, file.path(derived, 'predictions.rds'))
```

Storing the held-out predictions lets the figures and tables be
regenerated without refitting, which matters when refitting is
expensive.

### Discrimination, calibration, and the threshold

```{r}
#| label: adni-performance
auc <- function(y, p) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y)
  n0 <- sum(!y)
  (sum(r[y]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

auc_test <- auc(test$converted_3y, p_test)
auc_boot <- replicate(1000, {
  i <- sample(nrow(test), replace = TRUE)
  auc(test$converted_3y[i], p_test[i])
})

lp <- qlogis(p_test)
cal_slope <- coef(glm(test$converted_3y ~ lp, family = binomial))[['lp']]
cal_intercept <- coef(glm(test$converted_3y ~ offset(lp),
                          family = binomial))[[1]]

youden <- vapply(sort(unique(p_train)), \(t) {
  mean(p_train[train$converted_3y] >= t) +
    mean(p_train[!train$converted_3y] < t) - 1
}, numeric(1))
threshold <- sort(unique(p_train))[which.max(youden)]
flagged <- p_test >= threshold
y <- test$converted_3y

round(c(
  auc = auc_test, auc_lower = quantile(auc_boot, 0.025, names = FALSE),
  auc_upper = quantile(auc_boot, 0.975, names = FALSE),
  calibration_slope = cal_slope, calibration_intercept = cal_intercept,
  threshold = threshold,
  sensitivity = mean(flagged[y]), specificity = mean(!flagged[!y]),
  ppv = mean(y[flagged]), npv = mean(!y[!flagged])
), 2)
```

The AUC is computed in its rank-sum form, the probability that a
randomly chosen converter has a higher predicted risk than a
randomly chosen non-converter. The calibration slope is the
coefficient of the logit of the predicted risk in a logistic
regression of the outcome on it, and the calibration intercept is
that regression's intercept with the slope fixed at 1; a slope
below 1 means the predictions are too extreme, above 1 too
cautious. @fig-adni-calibration shows calibration directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-adni-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the held-out predictions: observed
#|   conversion proportion against mean predicted risk, by fifth of
#|   predicted risk, with 95% confidence intervals. Synthetic data."
#| fig-alt: "Calibration plot with predicted risk on the horizontal
#|   axis and observed proportion converted on the vertical axis,
#|   both from 0 to 1. Five points with vertical interval bars lie
#|   near the dashed diagonal line of perfect calibration, rising
#|   from low predicted risk to high."
#| fig-scap: "Calibration of held-out predictions"
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 4
calibration <- predictions |>
  mutate(fifth = ntile(predicted, 5)) |>
  group_by(fifth) |>
  summarize(predicted = mean(predicted), observed = mean(observed),
            n = n(), .groups = 'drop') |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / n))

ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 'dashed', color = 'grey50') +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = pmax(0, observed - 1.96 * se),
                      ymax = pmin(1, observed + 1.96 * se))) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = 'Mean predicted risk', y = 'Observed proportion converted') +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that no participant is in both the training and the test
set, that the folds cover every training participant, and that the
performance numbers come from the test set alone.

```{r}
#| label: adni-model-verify
stopifnot(
  length(intersect(train$RID, test$RID)) == 0,
  nrow(train) + nrow(test) == nrow(analytic_cohort),
  length(foldid) == nrow(train),
  all(table(foldid) >= floor(nrow(train) / 10)),
  nrow(predictions) == nrow(test)
)
```

These numbers recover the generator's parameters and are a check
on the code. They are not evidence about Alzheimer's disease, and
must never be reported as such.
:::

### Exercises

4. Suppose the modeling frame held every visit before month 12,
   several rows per participant. Assign ten folds at the
   participant level, and verify that no `RID` appears in more than
   one fold and that fold sizes are roughly equal.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-24-4
early_visits <- adnimerge_clean |>
  filter(visit_month < 12)

set.seed(7)
rid_fold <- tibble(RID = unique(early_visits$RID)) |>
  mutate(fold = sample(rep_len(1:10, n())))
early_visits <- left_join(early_visits, rid_fold, by = 'RID',
                          relationship = 'many-to-one')

folds_per_rid <- early_visits |>
  distinct(RID, fold) |>
  count(RID)
stopifnot(all(folds_per_rid$n == 1))
table(early_visits$fold)
```

Folds are assigned to participants, then joined to visits, so a
participant's rows travel together. Fold sizes in rows vary a
little, because participants contribute different numbers of
visits; in participants they differ by at most one. Assigning
`sample(rep_len(1:10, nrow(early_visits)))` to rows instead would
put most participants' two visits in different folds, and the
`stopifnot()` would fail.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Observation-level folds on a frame with two visits
per participant give an AUC of 0.88; participant-level folds give
0.74. Which do you report, and why is the first one higher?

**Answer.** Report 0.74. With observation-level folds, a
participant's second visit sits in the test fold while the first
trained the model, and the two visits are nearly identical, so the
model is partly recognizing people it has seen. A new patient is
never someone the model has seen, so only participant-level
validation estimates the performance the family in the opening
would get.
:::

## Reporting and deposit {#sec-adni-report}

### Reporting against TRIPOD+AI

The manuscript lives at `analysis/paper/paper.qmd`. Its
frontmatter uses a journal format from a Quarto journal extension
(installed with `quarto use template` or `quarto add`; `rticles`
provides the equivalent templates for R Markdown, not Quarto) and
the bibliography from `references.bib`. A prediction model is
reported against TRIPOD+AI (Transparent Reporting of a
multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or
Diagnosis, updated for artificial intelligence), whose 27-item
checklist supersedes TRIPOD 2015 for regression and machine
learning models alike [@collins2024tripodai]. @tbl-adni-tripod maps
selected items, grouped by domain, to the place in the compendium
that supplies them; the statement itself is the checklist to
submit.

| Domain | What to report | Where the compendium supplies it |
|---|---|---|
| Title and abstract | Development of a prediction model with internal validation; population, predictors, outcome | `paper.qmd` |
| Data and participants | Source (ADNI phases, dates), eligibility, the flow with counts | `01-build-cohort.R`; @tbl-adni-flow |
| Outcome | Conversion within three years: definition, ascertainment, handling of incomplete follow-up | SAP; `build_cohort()` |
| Predictors | The eight baseline predictors, defined and measured at baseline | SAP; @tbl-adni-vars |
| Sample size | Participants and events in training and test | @tbl-adni-flow; `04-model.R` |
| Missing data | Method and numbers excluded | SAP; @tbl-adni-flow |
| Analysis | Model class, tuning, participant-level resampling, holdout | `04-model.R` |
| Performance | Discrimination with CI; calibration plot, slope, intercept | `predictions.rds`; @fig-adni-calibration |
| Fairness | Performance in relevant subgroups, such as sex | Exploratory analyses, labeled |
| Model specification | The fitted model in full, so that others can apply it | Coefficients at `lambda.min` |
| Open science | Protocol or SAP, code availability, data access route | Zenodo deposit; README; the DUA route |

: Selected TRIPOD+AI reporting items mapped to the compendium.
{#tbl-adni-tripod}

### What gets deposited

| Deposit | Contents | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Zenodo (public) | Code, scripts, paper, README, Dockerfile, `renv.lock`, the synthetic generator with its assertions | Open; this DOI is what the paper cites |
| Container registry | The built Docker image | Open; `docker pull` from the registry |
| ADNI | The data | Under the DUA only |

: The two-part deposit for a DUA-restricted analysis.
{#tbl-adni-deposit}

Collaborators with DUA access run the full analysis; reviewers
without it run every script against the synthetic generator. Make
that the default: `scripts/01-build-cohort.R` should read the
frozen ADNI file when it exists and call the generator in
`scripts/00-simulate.R` when it does not, saying which it used.

### Verifying reproducibility

Before submitting, in a `zzcollab` project (display-only; the
tool-neutral equivalents are in @sec-zzcollab-audit):

```bash
make check-renv-no-fix      # code, DESCRIPTION, and renv.lock agree
make docker-rebuild         # the image builds without the cache
make docker-render REPORT=analysis/paper/paper.qmd
```

Then, on a colleague's machine: `git clone`, `make docker-build`,
and the same render. Expect bit-identical output for the
deterministic parts and rounding-level differences only where
floating-point order matters.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer without ADNI access reruns your
compendium and gets an AUC of `r round(auc_test, 2)`, different
from the paper's. Is the compendium broken?

**Answer.** Not necessarily: they ran the synthetic generator,
whose AUC reflects its own parameters. The check they can make is
that every script runs and every assertion passes. The README
should say this in so many words, and the paper should never
report a synthetic number, so that no reader can mistake one for
the other.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** Lock predictors, model,
   validation, and metrics in the SAP, and tag it before the cohort
   is built.
2. **Habit 8: a plausible number is the expensive bug.** Dropouts
   counted as non-converters give a lower risk that looks entirely
   reasonable; the `outcome_observed` filter and its assertion make
   the choice loud.
3. **Habit 12: send structure, not data.** Under a DUA, the
   schema, the synthetic generator, and aggregates are all a model
   or a reviewer ever needs to see.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-testing).* Write a `tinytest` file for
   `build_cohort()` with a fixture of four synthetic participants:
   one who converted at month 24 and then left, one followed
   through month 36 without converting, one who left after month
   12 without converting, and one who converted at month 48.
   Assert `outcome_observed` and `converted_by_3y` for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-24-5
fixture_visits <- function(rid, months, dx) {
  tibble(
    RID = rid, VISCODE = ifelse(months == 0, 'bl',
                                sprintf('m%02d', months)),
    EXAMDATE = as.Date('2012-01-01') + round(months * 30.44),
    DX_bl = 'LMCI', DX = dx, AGE = 70, PTGENDER = 'Female',
    PTEDUCAT = 16L, APOE4 = 1L, ADAS13 = 18, RAVLT.immediate = 30L,
    MMSE = 27L, LDELTOTAL = 6L
  )
}
fixture <- bind_rows(
  fixture_visits(1, c(0, 12, 24), c('MCI', 'MCI', 'Dementia')),
  fixture_visits(2, c(0, 12, 24, 36), rep('MCI', 4)),
  fixture_visits(3, c(0, 6, 12), rep('MCI', 3)),
  fixture_visits(4, c(0, 12, 24, 36, 48),
                 c('MCI', 'MCI', 'MCI', 'MCI', 'Dementia'))
)
out <- arrange(build_cohort(fixture), RID)

library(tinytest)
expect_equal(out$converted_by_3y, c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
             info = 'only participant 1 converted within the window')
expect_equal(out$outcome_observed, c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
             info = 'the early leaver without conversion is unobserved')
```

Participant 1 shows that an early converter who left stays in as a
converter; participant 3 that an early leaver without conversion
is excluded; participant 4 that a conversion after the window is a
non-conversion within it, because the participant was followed
through month 36. Each fixture row is a decision from the SAP, so
the test file doubles as its executable specification.
:::

6. *On your own work (requires ADNI access, no key).* With an
   approved DUA, run the compendium against `ADNIMERGE` for a
   different outcome (for example, progression from CN to MCI),
   adapting the SAP, the cohort function, and its tests, and deposit
   the code-only compendium with its synthetic generator.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Synthetic stand-in | `simulate_adnimerge()` plus schema assertions | Code no reviewer can run |
| Outcome observed | `converted_by_3y \| last_dx_days >= horizon - tolerance` | Dropouts counted as non-converters |
| Cohort flow | Count after every `filter()` | Unreported selection |
| Table 1 | `tbl_summary(by = ..., type = list(APOE4 ~ 'categorical'))` | Means of counts; row p-values |
| Participant-level folds | Assign folds to `RID`, then join; `group_vfold_cv(group = RID)` | Leakage across folds |
| Penalized model | `cv.glmnet(x, y, family = 'binomial', foldid = foldid)` | Tuning on the test set |
| Discrimination | Rank-sum AUC with bootstrap CI | A point estimate without uncertainty |
| Calibration | `glm(y ~ qlogis(p), family = binomial)`; binned plot | Discrimination reported alone |
| DUA | Schema and aggregates only, `.gitignore` the data | Disclosure of participant rows |

: The ADNI case study at a glance. {#tbl-adni-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-24}

1. The question is: *can baseline sociodemographic, clinical, and
   neuropsychological measures predict conversion from MCI to AD
   within three years?* It is clinically meaningful because MCI is
   a heterogeneous state: only some people progress to AD on a
   meaningful timescale, and identifying those at highest risk
   enables targeted intervention trials and earlier counseling.
2. ADNI analyses carry three distinguishing features: a data-use
   agreement that prevents data sharing (so the public compendium
   is code-only, with a synthetic stand-in); long time horizons
   (years between analysis and reviewer response, during which the
   R ecosystem drifts); and a dataset that updates periodically
   with renamed variables. All three increase the value of
   Docker-pinned environments and `renv`-pinned package versions.
3. ADNIMERGE is long-format (one row per participant per visit),
   with mixed diagnostic labels and inconsistent visit codes across
   ADNI 1, GO, 2, and 3. Analytic cohorts require baseline-anchored
   follow-up windows, careful handling of participants who leave
   before the outcome window closes, and consistent visit
   alignment. The step most commonly overlooked is *handling
   dropouts correctly*: a participant who leaves after year 2
   without converting has not been observed for the three-year
   outcome. Censor them in a time-to-event analysis, or exclude
   them and state that exclusion overstates the risk; never treat
   them as non-converters.
